messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Alvarez is a 28-year-old prison guard who came to treatment months after the sudden death of his younger brother, who was killed in a car crash late at night while driving home alone. Mateo had been the person in the family everyone called steady and protective, and in the days after the death he became fixated on the fact that his brother had called earlier that evening and Mateo had not picked up because he was on shift. He returns to that detail again and again. In his mind, if he had answered, if he had kept him talking, if he had insisted he wait until morning, his brother might still be alive. What has settled in most deeply is not only grief but a harsh conviction that he failed at the one thing he was supposed to do: protect the people he loves.

Since the death, reminders of loss have become difficult to tolerate in ways that feel immediate and bodily. At work, the prison break room television often runs local news, and when a segment mentions a fatal crash or a family speaking about someone they have lost, Mateo feels the room go strangely far away. He describes a detached, unreal sensation, as if he is still standing there but not fully inside himself. In those moments he pulls his hands over his face, partly to block out the screen and partly to hide what is happening to him from other officers. He has also begun steering away from almost anything that reminds him of his brother or of bereavement more broadly, changing the channel, walking out when coworkers start talking about somebody’s funeral, refusing family conversations that turn toward memories. When he cannot get away cleanly, he sometimes picks an argument instead—snapping over minor things, escalating with his wife or a coworker—because anger feels more manageable than that sliding, unreal feeling.

These moments do more than upset him; they confirm the conclusions he has drawn about himself. Hearing stories about other people losing loved ones or feeling that sudden detachment can bring back, with full force, the belief that he is a man who did not protect his brother and that whatever used to be hopeful or light in him is gone for good. He says he used to be a happy person and now feels miserable almost all the time. The future, when he imagines it at all, looks flat and empty. That conviction follows him into ordinary settings. During intake he described standing in the prison corridor after hearing an inmate mention his dead mother during a phone call, and immediately thinking, not just of his brother, but of himself as someone marked by failure and with nothing ahead except more of the same.

Over time, those beliefs have begun shaping what catches his attention. Because he has come to expect pain and see himself through this lens of failed protection and permanent misery, talk of loss jumps out at him everywhere. The news in the staff room, a passing conversation about a death in another officer’s family, even the first hint of feeling unreal in his own body all register as signs that he is not okay and may never be okay. He listens for them without meaning to. The world has narrowed around themes of death and absence.

His ways of coping have made that narrowing worse. Avoiding grief reminders has left him increasingly cut off from his wife and extended family; he leaves the room when they want to talk about his brother, and afterward he takes his withdrawal as proof that happiness and closeness are over for him. Covering his face at work spares him a few moments of exposure, but it also reinforces his sense that these reactions are dangerous and shameful, something that must be hidden. The arguments he starts to distract himself bring brief relief, yet afterward he feels guilty, exhausted, and more convinced that he has become someone miserable to live with. Each of these habits seems to deepen the same bleak appraisal: that he failed, that he has changed permanently, that there is no real future to recover into.

They also leave him more easily thrown the next time something brushes against loss. Because he avoids reminders, even a short news clip can hit him with greater force. Because conflict has become one of the few ways he knows to escape the ache, tension at home and on the job keeps him keyed toward the next upsetting exchange. Because he hides his face and waits for the detached feeling to pass, the feeling itself has become a trigger he dreads and notices immediately.

Mateo sought help after his wife told him she no longer recognized him and after a recent shift in which a television report about a fatal accident left him frozen and unreal in the break room, hands over his face, before he picked a fight with a coworker who asked if he was all right. What frightens him most is that this is all that remains of him now: the brother who failed, the husband who brings home anger, the man with no future. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget his brother, but to be able to hear about loss without disappearing inside it.
